name: Ochre Manuscript
description: Ochre Manuscript is a large desert world painted in the warm earth tones that give it its name—burnt orange plains, sienna canyon walls, and dust seas of pale ochre that glow amber at sunrise and deepen to chocolate brown at dusk. The planet's size supports a breathable atmosphere despite the arid conditions, and the massive canyon systems channel the wind into reliable patterns that desert-adapted fauna have learned to exploit. Mountain ranges along the continental margins catch what little moisture the atmosphere carries, creating narrow fertile zones where the desert briefly relents.

The fauna of Ochre Manuscript are tough, efficient organisms adapted to extremes of heat, cold, and aridity. The largest are burrowing creatures that excavate tunnel networks in the canyon walls, their activity over millions of years contributing to the canyon systems' extraordinary depth and complexity. Smaller organisms ride the wind currents between the mountain-edge oases, their life cycles timed to the brief moisture events that occur with seasonal regularity. The ecosystem is lean but resilient, having survived multiple climate shifts that are recorded in the canyon wall strata like paragraphs in a geological manuscript.

A warship of unknown origin crashed in the northern dust sea approximately three hundred years ago, its impact creating a secondary crater that has since been half-filled with windblown sand. The ship is massive—over two kilometers in length—and its design suggests a military vessel of considerable capability, though its armaments and power systems have long since been depleted or degraded. No matching vessel type exists in any accessible military database, and the ship's crew was never found, leading to speculation that it operated autonomously.

Ochre Manuscript's breathable atmosphere and moderate gravity make it one of the more hospitable desert worlds, and settlement proposals surface regularly. The warship crash site is the primary complication—its reactor core, though degraded, still emits low-level radiation, and the hull contains materials of potential military application that have attracted the attention of both governments and arms dealers. The fauna continue their ancient patterns around and through the wreck, having incorporated the crashed ship into their ecosystem with the same pragmatic efficiency they apply to every other obstacle the desert provides.
